title: LLM Inference & Serving Engines, Mapped by Failure Mode
description: A curated reference of self-hosted LLM inference and serving engines, organized by the production failure each one prevents — throughput collapse, prefix recompute, tail latency, hardware waste and edge deployment.
standfirst: For platform and ML engineers running open-weight models on their own hardware — organized by how serving actually fails under real traffic, not by tokens-per-second on a single prompt.
hook: Inference engines aren't ranked by peak tokens per second — they're ranked by what happens at p99 when the 500th concurrent agent sends the same 8k-token prefix.

exclusions.intro: Serving is the layer where benchmarks lie most. A single-request throughput chart tells you nothing about batching, cache reuse or the tail.

items.name: Engines in maintenance mode
items.reason: Hugging Face's Text Generation Inference entered maintenance mode in December 2025 and itself recommends vLLM or SGLang. An existing TGI deployment need not be ripped out, but it is not a default for new systems.

items.name: Hosted inference APIs
items.reason: managed endpoints solve a procurement problem, not a serving-architecture one; they belong in the gateway and routing reference, not here.

items.name: Research prototypes without a server
items.reason: a kernel or scheduling paper with a demo script is not something you can put behind a load balancer. If it matters, it usually lands inside vLLM or SGLang within a release or two.

items.name: Generic model servers with no LLM-specific scheduling
items.reason: a server that runs one request per forward pass, with no continuous batching or KV-cache management, wastes most of the GPU on autoregressive workloads.

exclusions.bar: an OpenAI-compatible (or equivalent) server, continuous batching or an explicit reason it is unnecessary, and a release inside the research window.

failure_modes.title: Throughput Collapses Under Concurrency
failure_modes.body: The demo serves one user beautifully. At fifty concurrent requests, naive serving pads batches to the longest sequence, fragments KV-cache memory and leaves the GPU idle between tokens. Cost per token climbs exactly when usage succeeds.

tools.name: vLLM
tools.fit: PagedAttention for KV-cache memory, continuous batching, automatic prefix caching and the broadest model and hardware coverage of any open engine; fits teams that want one default engine across many models and accelerators, not teams chasing the last few percent on a single fixed model.
tools.limit: fast-moving releases mean configuration flags and defaults change often — pin versions and re-benchmark on upgrade.

failure_modes.title: Agents Recompute the Same Prefix on Every Turn
failure_modes.body: Agent and multi-turn workloads resend a long system prompt, tool schema and conversation history on every call. Without cache reuse across requests, the engine re-runs prefill on thousands of identical tokens per turn — the most expensive tokens are the ones it already saw.

tools.name: SGLang
tools.fit: RadixAttention keeps a radix tree of KV caches so shared prefixes are reused across requests automatically, with a frontend language for structured multi-call programs; fits agentic, multi-turn and tree-of-calls workloads with heavy prefix overlap, not one-shot batch jobs with unique prompts.
tools.limit: the biggest wins depend on prefix overlap in your real traffic — measure the cache hit rate before crediting the engine.

failure_modes.title: Prefill Bursts Wreck Tail Latency at Scale
failure_modes.body: One long-context prefill stalls every decode stream sharing that GPU. Round-robin load balancing then sends the next request to a replica that has none of its prefix cached. At cluster scale, p99 latency is a scheduling problem — routing, disaggregation and cache placement — not a kernel problem.

tools.name: NVIDIA Dynamo
tools.fit: Datacenter-scale serving layer that disaggregates prefill and decode onto separate workers, moves KV cache between them with NIXL and routes requests by KV-cache overlap; fits multi-node GPU fleets serving large models where tail latency is the SLO, not a single-GPU deployment.
tools.limit: it orchestrates engines (vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM) rather than replacing them, so you operate both layers.

tools.name: llm-d
tools.fit: Kubernetes-native distributed inference with inference-aware routing, prefill/decode disaggregation and hierarchical KV offload, built on vLLM; a CNCF Sandbox project since March 2026. Fits platform teams who want inference scheduling to be Kubernetes primitives, not a separate control plane.
tools.limit: young project (v0.x) — expect APIs and Helm values to move.

failure_modes.title: Leaving Performance on Expensive Hardware
failure_modes.body: When the model is fixed and the fleet is large, every percent of throughput is real money. General-purpose engines trade peak performance for flexibility; at enough scale that trade inverts.

tools.name: TensorRT-LLM
tools.fit: NVIDIA's optimised runtime with fused kernels, FP8/FP4 quantisation paths and in-flight batching for NVIDIA GPUs; fits large, stable deployments of a few models on NVIDIA hardware where peak efficiency justifies extra build complexity, not heterogeneous fleets or fast model churn.
tools.limit: NVIDIA-only, and new model architectures can land later than in vLLM or SGLang.

failure_modes.title: There Is No Datacenter GPU Where the Model Has to Run
failure_modes.body: Air-gapped sites, laptops, on-device assistants and cost-sensitive internal tools often have CPUs, Apple silicon or one consumer GPU. Datacenter engines assume CUDA and gigabytes of headroom; here the failure is that the model does not run at all.

tools.name: llama.cpp
tools.fit: C/C++ inference with GGUF quantisation across CPU, Metal, CUDA, Vulkan and more, plus a built-in OpenAI-compatible server; fits edge, offline and developer-machine deployments where portability beats throughput, not high-concurrency serving.
tools.limit: concurrency and batching are modest compared with datacenter engines.

tools.name: Ollama
tools.fit: Packages local models with one-command pulls, a model registry and a local API; fits developer workstations and small internal tools that need a model running in minutes, not production multi-tenant serving.
tools.limit: convenience defaults (context size, quantisation) hide choices you will eventually need to make explicitly.

missing: There is still no neutral, reproducible benchmark for realistic serving: mixed context lengths, prefix overlap, bursty arrivals and an SLO on p99 time-to-first-token. Every vendor publishes its own harness. KV-cache portability across engines is also unsolved — a cache built by one engine cannot be served by another, which keeps disaggregated and tiered caching locked to a single stack. Until those exist, run your own traffic replay before believing anyone's chart.
choose: Default to vLLM or SGLang for a new deployment and let measurements move you off it. Run both on a replay of your own traffic — real prompt lengths, real concurrency, real prefix overlap — and compare time-to-first-token and inter-token latency at p50 and p99, not peak throughput. The engine that wins on a single long prompt often loses on fifty short agent turns.

Add a cluster layer such as Dynamo or llm-d only when a single replica's tail latency, or cache misses caused by naive load balancing, is the measured bottleneck. Disaggregation is real engineering with real operational cost; it pays off on large models and large fleets, and rarely before. TensorRT-LLM earns its build complexity when the model is stable and the GPU bill is large enough that ten percent matters.

Keep the serving API OpenAI-compatible at the boundary, whichever engine is behind it. That one decision lets your gateway, evals and cost tooling stay unchanged when you switch engines — and in this layer you will switch engines, because the leader changes every few releases.
